assail

/uh-SAYL/ - rhymes with sail · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Assail means to attack vigorously with blows or words.

The moment tickets went on sale, angry season-holders assailed the box office with calls, emails, and one hand-delivered spreadsheet.

Example

When the museum unveiled the restored fresco, purists assailed the restoration in every journal, calling the brightened sky 'a vandalism of memory.'

Assail means to attack in waves — blows, questions, or criticisms arriving hard and fast from every side. You criticize a decision once; you assail it when you batter it relentlessly. The word's picture is physical: a leap at the target.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

attack: Attack is the plain, general word for going after a target — a single punch or one harsh review is an attack. Assail multiplies it: the blows or criticisms come in waves, from every side, without letup. You can attack once; to assail is to keep the attacks coming.

bombard: To bombard is to overwhelm with a continuous stream — questions, emails, artillery — and the word cares only about volume. Assail adds intent to damage: an assailed target is under hostile attack, not merely flooded. Fans bombard a star with friendly requests; hostile critics assail her performance.

lambaste: To lambaste is to thrash someone in words alone — one scathing review or furious editorial can lambaste. Assail is broader and bigger: it covers verbal and physical sieges alike, and its signature is attack arriving from every side. One critic lambastes a film; a whole chorus of critics assails it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

defend: protect a person or position from attack

shield: physically or figuratively block harm from reaching someone

Where it sits · how hard the challenge presses

question → criticize → assail

question vs. assail: To question a plan is the gentlest challenge there is, far short of assailing it.

criticize vs. assail: Criticize finds faults one at a time; it stops short of assail, which batters the target from every side at once.

Which word fits?

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — as-: at, toward (a form of ad-)

Root — sail: to leap (Latin salire)

Put it together: As- (at) + sail (to leap) = to leap at someone. Latin assilire meant to spring upon; an assailant still leaps, and to assail an argument is to jump on it from every side. No relation to a ship's sail — that word is plain Old English.

Use the root in a new word: assault: The castle withstood the assault — the attackers' leap at its walls — for nine days.

Word Building

Word Choice

formal / vivid

Assail turns criticism into a siege — use it when attacks come in volleys, physical or verbal. Its unit-mates divide the labor: berate targets a person to their face at length, rail vents loudly against something, and assail presses an attack meant to damage.
